Chapter 2: Literature Review 
Humans are social creatures. Humans have formed organizations since our 
species learned to reason, but organizations as we know them today have evolved 
significantly over the last several hundred years. 
Organizations can be incredibly complex, and their management and design 
require art and science skills. The socio-technical nature of today’s organizations 
introduces unique managerial, design, and structural challenges for new and existing 
organizations. 
To better understand the challenges surrounding organizations and their 
management, this chapter explores the background and relevant literature that lay the 
foundation for today’s state of the art in this focus area.  
This chapter is structured in three main sections. The first section highlights what 
organizations are, organizational theory, and the theoretical underpinnings that have 
been broadly accepted as descriptive of complex organizations. The second section 
discusses organizational design and existing techniques academics and practitioners 
offer to design or analyze organizations.  The final section of this review delves into 
Systems Theory. This section highlights the attributes of organizations as complex 
systems and provides an overview of systems-theoretic analysis or modeling techniques 
that have been developed and leveraged in other application domains. 
2.1   Organizations and Organizational Theory   
2.1.1 Organizations  
  
So, what is an organization? There are several definitions in the literature about 
what an organization is. Edgar Schein, a leading researcher in the field of organizational 
behavior, said an organization “is the planned coordination of activities of a number of 
people for the achievement of some common, explicit purpose or goal, through division 
of labor and function, and through a hierarchy of authority and responsibility”[9], [10].  
  
To Ralph Davis, a mid-century organizational theorist, “an organization is a group 
of people working together under a leader to accomplish an objective”[10], [11]. 
  
A modern organizational theorist, Richard Daft, offered that organizations “are 
social entities that are goal-directed, are designed as deliberately structured and 
coordinated activity systems, and are linked to the external environment"[12].  

15 
 
 
 
 
  
These three leading definitions vary in detail about what an organization is. Still, 
they agree that an organization involves a structured group of people working together 
toward a common goal.   
  
The organization also has many synonyms, and this linguistic phenomenon 
highlights the ubiquitous nature of the concept in humans. Other terms for an 
organization include team, enterprise, union, group, coalition, corporation, association, 
federation, firm, and network. This thesis will use the word organization to clarify this 
important concept. 
2.1.2 Organizational Theory 
 
Organizational Theory is a transdisciplinary field that “encapsulates a range of 
perspectives from economics, psychology, and sociology [9]. Suter et al., organizational 
researchers, stated, “Organizational Theory focuses on the holistic examination of 
organizations, i.e., the study of organization from multiple viewpoints, using multiple 
methods and levels of analysis”[13]. More simply, it studies how organizations work and 
interact with their environment.  
 
The breadth of organization theory makes it essential to understand and use 
because it is a way to see and think about organizations [12]. Herbert Simon, a leading 
organizational behavior theorist, “envisaged ‘organization theory’ as a broad category 
that included scientific management, industrial engineering, industrial psychology, the 
psychology of small groups, human-resources management, and strategy [14], [15]. By 
understanding and applying the various concepts of organizational theory, leaders can 
effectively analyze, design, or redesign their organizations to be more effective. 
 
Organizational Theory did not develop until the late 19th century; it is a relatively 
new field of study because the need to study organizations was not needed until the 
Industrial Revolution began to change the world.  Despite being relatively new, there 
have been four key periods of evolution since its inception; the theories, concepts, and 
frameworks developed during these times can be categorized as classical, neoclassical, 
modernist, and postmodern organizational theory. The subsequent subsections examine 
each of these eras.  
2.1.2.1 Classical Organizational Theory 
Classical organizational theory occurred between the late 19th and early 20th 
centuries. This period was brought on by the rise of the Industrial Revolution, which led 
to the seminal works of Frederick Taylor (scientific management), Max Weber 
(bureaucratic management), and Henri Fayol (administrative management). The key 
concepts of this era include efficiency, hierarchy, clear division of labor, and formal 
structures. The characteristics of the theories developed by these gentlemen are centered 

16 
 
 
 
 
around task specialization and standardization, hierarchical structures with clear lines of 
authority, and a focus on efficiency and control through formal rules and procedures. 
These three thought leaders and their pioneering theories laid the foundation for 
organizational theory, and many elements of their work are still in use today.  
Fredrick Taylor, the father of scientific management, was responsible for 
developing scientific management, which focused on optimizing worker productivity 
and streamlining production processes through scientific analysis. Through scientific 
methods, “one best way” to do the work could be identified and exploited for the 
organization’s benefit  [16]. Taylor’s “one best way” would have a lasting impact on 
organizational and management theory.  
  
Max Weber, “who initiated the contemporary sociological study of bureaucracy, 
freed the word from pejorative connotations and stressed the essentiality of bureaucracy 
for the rational achievement of the aims of the organizations [17]. He “considered the 
organization of broader society. He looked at the structure of the organization and the 
control of member behavior” [17]. Weber’s bureaucratic management focused on 
developing organizations in an objective and logical way, specifically with clear lines of 
authority, responsibility, and accountability. 
 
Henri Fayol, a French engineer and manager in the mining industry, authored the 
book General and Industrial Management in 1919. Fayol outlined six key functions of 
management and fourteen management principles in his book. Fayol’s work essentially 
established the field of administration management, which focuses on “the design and 
functioning of the organization as a whole” [12], [17]. The output of Fayol’s work is still 
used in practice today.  
2.1.2.2 Neoclassical Organizational Theory  
  
The next critical time for organization theory was from the 1930s to the 1950s, 
known as the neoclassical era. The neoclassical era arose primarily because the classical 
era ignored the human worker or treated the human worker as a machine. This lack of 
acknowledgment of the impact of the human worker on the organization and the 
organization on the human worker gave way to the rise of the neoclassical era. American 
organizational theorist J.L. Bowditch claimed that “the neoclassical school of thought can 
be viewed as a critique of the classical doctrine” [16], [18], [19]. This is evident in the key 
concepts developed during this era: human relations, worker satisfaction, and informal 
structures.  
 
A critical foundation of the neoclassical school of thought is the Hawthorne 
studies, led by Elton Mayo, F.J. Roethlisberger, and William J. Dickinson. In 1927, Mayo 
and his associates led a research study at the Chicago Western Electric Company’s 

17 
 
 
 
 
Hawthorne Works site [20]. The focus of the studies was to understand behavior in the 
workplace specifically as it pertains to “style of leadership, working conditions and other 
organizational issues with employee output”[21], [22], [23]. The outcome of these 
experiments was the importance of the human element in the workplace. Especially the 
notion that treating workers well increases their motivation and ultimately benefits the 
organization's productivity. 
  
The Hawthorne studies “underlined that the group dynamics and social makeup 
of an organization were an extremely crucial force either for or against higher 
productivity. This outcome caused the call for greater participation from the workers, 
greater trust and openness in the working environment, and great attention to teams and 
groups in the workplace [16]. The work of these experiments laid the foundation for 
human relations and understanding the impact of informal structures. 
  
Another thought leader during this time was Mary Parker Follet, an American 
management scholar, social worker, and government consultant. Mary’s contribution to 
the development of organization theory revolves around the idea that employees know 
their job best and, therefore, managers should leverage their worker’s expertise to 
improve work processes and functions. Follett’s idea directly challenged Frederick 
Taylor’s scientific management theory and highlighted the importance of a humane side 
of organization and involving the worker [24]. Mary’s work led to behavior management 
theory, which “refers to how managers ought to behave in motivating employees to 
become committed to achieving organizational goals and objectives” [24]. Her work 
contributed to the humanization of management and management practices. 
  
Mary Parker Follett’s work helped inspire some of Chester Barnard’s ideas on the 
role of the executive in an organization, which he published in 1938 in The Functions of the 
Executive. Barnard, an American management theorist, believed that the role of an 
executive should be focused on developing and maintaining the organization’s purpose, 
ensuring the organization was appropriately resourced, and tending to the organization’s 
structure, roles, responsibilities, and relationships. It is evident in Barnard’s work that he 
recognized that the role of executives was to nurture the organization specifically by 
recognizing it as a social system and focusing on effective communication and motivating 
employees [25].  
2.1.2.3 Modern Organizational Theory 
 
Just as the neoclassical era addressed the shortcomings of classical organization 
theory, the modern organization theory era has further developed and expanded upon 
neoclassical ideas, filling in the gaps and advancing the field even further. The timeframe 
of the modern movement of organization theory began around the mid-20th century and 

18 
 
 
 
 
lasted until approximately 2010.  This period of the theory can be summarized in two 
words: integration and holistic-ness; “modern organization theory is an integration of 
valuable concepts of classical models with the social and behavioral sciences”, “it is the 
study of the organization as a whole” [26], [27]. The dominant ideas which emerged were 
systems theory, contingency theory, bounded rationality, and socio-technical theory.  
A primary idea during this era was that the organization is a system. The roots of 
this idea come from the notion that all aspects of the natural and social world can be 
described as systems.  This concept, called General Systems Theory, is generally 
attributed to Viennese theoretical biologist Ludwig von Bertalanffy [28]. Von 
Bertalanffy’s “ideas were based on the observation that societies contain groups, groups 
contain individuals, individuals are comprised of organs, organs of cells, cells of 
molecules, molecules of atoms, and so on. Von Bertalanffy considered each of these 
phenomena, which have their own dedicated science, to be a system, and he sought the 
laws and principles generic to all of them” [25].  
He developed the concept of a “system” as an antidote to the limitations of 
individual disciplines in addressing complex social problems [13], [29]. Simply put, 
system theorists believe all systems, whether scientific, engineered, or social, all have the 
same basic elements, such as hierarchy and control.  A more detailed review of Systems 
Theory will be provided in section 2.3.  To understand systems theory pertaining to 
organizations and organization theory, Suter et al. stated, “the basic premise of systems 
theory is that organizations consist of multiple, interdependent parts that collectively 
form more than the sum of their parts. Interactions between parts of the system are seen 
as purposeful, boundaries are permeable, and cause and effect as dynamic, nonlinear 
process”[13]. This notion gave rise to the saying, “the sum is greater than its parts”.  
Another theory that arose in the 1960s that has shaped organization theory is 
contingency theory. Contingency theory arose out of the limitations of classical theory, 
specifically the fundamental idea championed by Frederick Taylor that science can be 
used to find the best way to organize work for organizations. The basic concept of 
contingency theory is that there is no one-size-fits-all approach to organizational design, 
and that organization's design must consider the circumstance and context in which it 
exists [24], [30]. Paul Lawrence and Jay Lorsch primarily led this theory’s development.  
Bounded rationality is another fundamental concept of organization theory 
developed during the mid-century by Herbert Simon and James March. This concept 
arose as a critique of the classical theories of scientific management and economics, which 
theorized that  “a rational individual has unlimited cognitive capabilities, and his choice 
of behavior is focused on maximizing his own expected utility”[31], [32]. Simon, in his 
1947 book entitled Administrative Behavior: a Study of Decision-Making Processes in 

19 
 
 
 
 
Administrative Organization, stated, “at the base of the real human behavior, there are 
three restrictions on cognition: incompleteness of information, difficulty in the 
anticipation of the consequences of future actions; and scarce knowledge of all possible 
human behaviors”[31], [33], [34]. In response to his findings, Simon developed the 
bounded rationality model with March’s help.  
Simon and March’s work showed “that the design of the organization was a 
strategy to deal with both lack of information and the inability of actors to be able to 
absorb endless amounts of information”[35]. Their work created a comprehensive 
approach to understanding organizations and their problems, such as how to structure 
themselves, motivate and track employee performance, and adapt to changing market 
conditions.  
Another critical theory that emerged was the socio-technical theory. This theory 
emerged in the 1960s over “the concern for the interaction between two organizational 
subsystems – social structure and technology” [25]. Eric Trist and Ken Bamforth 
established the theory through their work with the Tavistock Institute of Human 
Relations in the United Kingdom [25]. Their theory “aims to address problems associated 
with the introduction of new technologies in an organization”[13], [32]. It is focused on 
the intersection of an organization's social and technical aspects.  
The main principles of this theory are: 1) how well members of an organization 
work together and how well they use the technical tools (processes and tools) that can 
affect the success of an organization, and 2) focusing on only one of these elements can 
negatively impact the overall performance of the organization.   
2.1.2.4 Post-Modern Organizational Theory 
While modern organization theory focuses on viewing organizations as a system 
and looking at those systems as a whole, the postmodern era, which is in its infancy, 
focuses on how organizations are understood and how organizations can reconcile 
complexity and ambiguity. This evolution of the theory began to emerge in the late 20th 
century, and the initial focus and development of the theory has been on power, identity, 
and how communication occurs within an organization.   
While the modernist mentality on organizational theory relied heavily on control, 
order, and overall efficiency, the postmodern movement questions modern 
organizational design and theory tenets. Unlike the contemporary school of thinking, the 
“postmodern theory of organizational power demonstrates that we are empowered only 
through the actions of others”[36]. This construct insinuates that emphasizing power and 
influence should be abandoned in favor of concepts encouraging interdependence 
amongst stakeholders and members of today’s organizations. 

20 
 
 
 
 
Understanding the evolution of organization theory helps the reader understand 
key tenets of the approaches employed in the recent past and today in organizational 
design. As evident in this historical review of the evolution of organization theory, it is 
essential to remember that organization theory lays the foundation for how to see, 
analyze, and understand an organization.  
2.2   Organizational Design Methods 
  
Having established the foundations of organizational theory, this review now 
examines the practical application of organizational design. The effective design of an 
organization is imperative to its overall performance and adaptability; therefore, it is 
important to review the basic concepts, key elements, and frameworks that been 
developed to support this process. The aim is to understand how these approaches are 
employed and how they both help and hinder organizations that are  undergoing 
organizational design improvements.  
2.2.1 What is Organizational Design and Why it Matters 
Organizational design is about assembling elements, such as structure, people, 
and processes, to optimize the organization's operation efficiently and effectively. As 
noted by organizational theorists, Robert Burton and Borge Obel, “organization design is 
a systematic approach to aligning structures, processes, leadership, culture, people, 
practices, and metrics to enable organizations to achieve their mission and strategy”[37]. 
Effective organizational design matters because it directly impacts an organization’s 
ability to meet its goals.   
  
Without the right design, an organization’s performance can be undermined; an 
improper design or  “inappropriate attempts to introduce changes in organizational 
design also can be costly. They can disrupt a company’s operations, generate resistance 
and hostility among employees” and lead to several other organizational problems [1]. 
“good” organizational design creates value for those taking part in the organization, and 
for those using the products and services of that organization”[38]. Fundamentally, 
organizational design is about creating the proper structure and internal environment 
that allows an organization to operate effectively, meet its goals, and remain competitive.  
2.2.1.1 When Does Organizational Design Occur 
 
There are two overarching times organizational design should be considered for 
an organization. The most obvious is when an organization is forming. The other time 
organizational design practices and methods are needed is when the organizational 
needs are not being met, resulting in the organization requiring reorganization or 

21 
 
 
 
 
redesign. Typically, this occurs when the “organization structure is out of alignment with 
the organization’s needs” [12]. Leading indicators of structural deficiency are: decision-
making is delayed or lacking in quality, the organization does not respond innovatively 
to a changing environment, employee performance declines, goals are not being met, and 
too much conflict is evident [12], [39], [40]. Organizations need to understand these 
leading indicators to address any organizational issues proactively.  
2.2.2 Key Concepts of Organizational Design 
  
Regardless of who is designing an organization, the design effort focuses on 
making the organization the best it can be in the context of its environment to meet its 
goals. While many organizational design methods and frameworks exist, fundamental 
concepts must be understood and considered regardless of the framework used to aid the 
design efforts.  These concepts include organizational design dimensions and the basic 
parts and types of organizations.  
2.2.2.1 Organizational Design Dimensions 
One of the first elements anyone trying to design or redesign an organization 
should look at is the dimensions of the organization. Two types of dimensions should be 
considered: the structural dimension and the contextual dimension. These two 
dimensions provide essential information about the organization, allowing designers to 
evaluate and understand the organization [12]. Figure 1 shows how the dimensions are 
interdependent.

2.2.2.2 Organizational Structure Design Considerations  
  
When designing an organization, a key part is focused on developing the 
organizational structure. This focus on the structure is critical because structure directly 
impacts an organization’s ability to function effectively and accomplish its goals. It is 

25 
 
 
 
 
important to consider the structure's vertical or horizontal nature because these types of 
structuring fundamentally determine how an organization's authority, roles, and 
decision-making are defined. Each structure exhibits its own characteristics and tends to 
support specific organization types and operating environments. 
A vertical structure, which is the oldest of the two forms since it has direct ties to 
how organizations were shaped and managed since the Industrial Revolution and allows 
organizations to optimize for efficiency, is described by having a tall structure. The 
vertical nature of this structure is because there are typically multiple layers of 
management. Additionally, a vertical structure has a clear chain of command, centralized 
decision-making, and a communication flow that normally flows up and down the 
organizational hierarchy. In a vertical structure, roles and responsibilities are known to 
all employees.  This type of structure lends itself to organizations striving for efficiency, 
uniformity, and control. Organizations with a vertical structure typically operate in a 
stable environment where variability is rare or manageable.  Examples of organizations 
with vertical structures are militaries, governmental agencies, and mass production 
agencies.  
Vertical structures thrive in stable environments, “however, in a rapidly changing 
environment, the hierarchy becomes overloaded. Top executives are not able to respond 
rapidly enough to problems or opportunities”[12]. Other drawbacks to this type of 
structure are slowness to adopt change, slow communication, decision-making, and the 
potential for bureaucratic inefficiencies.   
A horizontal structure, otherwise known as a flat structure, is a relatively new type 
that only emerged in the late 20th century when a shift began from industrial 
manufacturing to service and knowledge-based industries. Service and knowledge-based 
organizations are not mass-production industrial organizations; therefore, they do not 
necessarily need to exhibit tight control of their organization to ensure efficiency.   
A horizontal structure usually has fewer management layers and decentralized 
decision-making, meaning employees have more capability and ability to make decisions 
without excessive approval.  Additionally, the work involves cross-functional knowledge 
from its employees. It leads to organizations that allow teams to form from within and 
have a wide variety of knowledge and experience.  
The benefits of a horizontal structure for an organization are their ability to adapt 
to change as needed to fit their operational environments, faster communication, easier 
collaboration, and innovation.  Horizontal structures are best for organizations that value 
innovation, exist in fluid operating environments, and are smaller in scale.  

26 
 
 
 
 
The drawbacks to a horizontal structure are that roles and responsibilities may not 
be as clearly defined as in a vertical structure, which can create ambiguity for all those 
involved, and it can be challenging to scale these types of organizations. 
It is worth noting that in today’s evolving and complex world, many organizations 
exhibit a combination of both structures. This combination certainly can help an 
organization achieve the best aspects of each structure. Still, it does induce greater 
complexity for an organization and requires the right leadership and organizational 
culture to manage and maintain effectively.   
2.2.2.2.1 Organizational Structure and Information Flow  
 
Another critical aspect of an organization’s structural design is information flow. 
According to Daft, “organization design should facilitate the communication among 
employees and departments that is necessary to accomplish the organization’s overall 
task”[12]. Information needs to flow vertically and horizontally in an organization. 
 
Vertical information flow or linkages “coordinate activities between the top and 
bottom of an organization and are designed primarily for control of the 
organization”[12]. These linkages are established through a chain of command, rules, 
plans, and reporting systems.  
 
Horizontal information flow or linkages “refers to communication and 
coordination horizontally across organizational departments. Horizontal communication 
overcomes barriers between departments and provides opportunities for coordination 
among employees to achieve” organizational goals [12]. The mechanisms to support 
horizontal information linkages are cross-functional information systems that all 
members of the organization can use, direct contact between managers of different 
departments, the establishment of liaison roles within each department whose 
responsibility is to ensure communication and coordination between departments, and 
the use of an integrator which can be a member or department outside of the other 
departments whose responsibility is coordination amongst multiple departments [12].  
 
Information flow is crucial to any organization; if the information flow does not 
match the information needs of the organization, then “people either will have too little 
information or will spend time processing information that is not vital to their tasks, thus 
reducing effectiveness”[12], [44]. Most organizations today establish vertical and 
horizontal information linkages and combine the abovementioned mechanisms to 
achieve effective communication, coordination, and collaboration. 
While the selection of structure and all the other elements addressed in this entire 
section is essential to consider while designing or redesigning an organization, “the most 
important decision that managers make about structural design is to find the right 

27 
 
 
 
 
balance between vertical control and horizontal coordination, depending on the needs of 
the organization” [1]. Striking the right balance and finding the structure and elements 
that fit the organization’s needs is imperative during the design process; otherwise, the 
organization will not be able to efficiently or effectively meet its goals.   
2.2.3 Leading Organizational Design Methods 
 
After outlining the fundamental concepts of organizational design, it is time to 
explore the leading models that guide the practical application of designing (or 
redesigning) an organization. Utilizing organizational design models is important 
because they provide a structured approach to helping people understand how an 
organization functions and how it could operate in the future. Models are simplify 
complex ideas, making it easier for everyone in the organization to understand, discuss, 
and design together [45].  
 
Numerous organizational design models exist, providing leaders and managers 
guidance and processes for designing or redesigning their organizations. The following 
section examines three notable methods: Galbraith’s Star Model, McKinsey 7-S, and the 
Burke-Litwin Model. 
These three models have been selected because of their comprehensive approaches 
to organizational design; they represent different perspectives of organizational design 
and are still utilized today.   
2.2.3.1 Galbraith’s Star Model 
Jay Galbraith was a leading scholar in the field of organization design and was the 
first to map organization strategy against structures, information-processing functions, 
reward systems, and people practices through his development of his Star Model in his 
1977 book, Organization Design [46].  
Galbraith’s Star Model provides a way to think holistically about the five 
components of organizational design. According to Galbraith, the five components are 
strategy, structure, processes, rewards, and people. His framework is displayed 
graphically as a star because the interconnecting lines highlight the importance of the five 
components, their interdependence, and how they must be aligned to enable an 
organization's best performance [46]. Galbraith’s Star Model is shown below in Figure 2.   

28 
 
 
 
 
Figure 2: Galbraith's Star Model [46], [47] 
Strategy informs the direction of the organization from what the organization 
produces or provides, what markets they are in, and how the organization will be 
profitable.  
Structure comprises the locus of power and where decisions are made.  
Processes determine information flow. Vertical and horizontal information flows 
determine how information flows up and down the chain of command and across the 
organization. 
Reward systems help motivate members to perform to reach the organization’s 
goals.   
People policies, otherwise known as human resource policies, establish guidance 
and standards for the management of organizational members.  

29 
 
 
 
 
Galbraith believed these five components were crucial to organizational design. 
He observed that too much emphasis was being placed on organizational structure 
during the design. Although he recognized the importance of structure, it was not the 
only element organizations should concern themselves with during the design process. 
It is important to note that Galbraith believed there is no “one size fits all” to 
organizational design, and each organization needs to build a design that works best for 
them.  
2.2.3.1.1 Galbraith’s Star Model Theoretical Background 
Herbert Simon, James March, Paul Lawrence, and Jay Lorsch strongly influenced 
Galbraith's work. Simon and March’s work on bounded rationality, which showed “there 
are limits to rational thinking in organizations and these limits have important 
consequences,” shaped a lot of Galbraith’s work, including the Star Model [46]. The Star 
Model accounts for bounded rationality through the structure and process components. 
Structure and process are interwoven and affect managers' and leaders' ability to make 
effective decisions for the organization; organizations should structure themselves in a 
way that helps decision-makers make informed decisions since these members have 
cognitive limits.  
Galbraith’s Star Model framework also draws upon contingency theory and the 
work done by Lawrence and Lorsch. He draws on contingency theory when he states that 
in Designing Organizations, “there is no “one size fits all” organizational design, and the 
design selected should be the one that best matches the strategy [47].   
2.2.3.1.2 Galbraith’s Star Model Application 
 
The Star Model is a tool and blueprint for leaders and managers designing an 
organization. By using this model, organizations can take a holistic approach to their 
design process and ensure they are aligning their organization in a way that allows them 
to maintain top performance. The Star Model can be used to address a variety of issues 
or opportunities for an organization. It is typically used during organizational 
restructuring to aid in change management, and it can address and improve an 
organization’s performance [48]. 
2.2.3.1.3 Galbraith’s Star Model Strengths, Limitations, and Critiques  
 
The strengths of Galbraith’s Star Model are its comprehensiveness through the five 
components that need to be considered and aligned to develop an organization that can 
perform well.  The Star Model can be applied to any organization, regardless of size or 
industry [48]. Additionally, the model is practical; it offers a clear and actionable 
framework for organizations. 

30 
 
 
 
 
 
Although the Star Model is comprehensive, it has some limitations worth 
highlighting. The first limitation is its lack of acknowledgment of how culture impacts 
the organizational design process and how it should be considered within the model. 
Another difficulty is that there is a lack of information on what constitutes alignment of 
the five components and how designers know if they have effectively aligned them.  
The issues organizations face today are complex; the model comes across as an 
oversimplification, and everything boils down to those five elements. Perhaps it is simply 
the passage of time, but those elements do not seem enough for today’s organizations. 
Additionally, there is a lack of consideration for how the environment should shape the 
design process.  
Finally, the model and literature on the model come across as relatively static. 
While Galbraith draws upon contingency theory for his model, information on when and 
how to re-evaluate the organizational design is lacking. 
2.2.3.2 McKinsey 7-S Model 
In the late 1970s, Tom Peters and Robert Waterman, two consultants at McKinsey 
& Company, a highly regarded management consulting company, developed the 7-S 
model. They created this model after working with several clients and consulting on their 
organizational problems. Peters and Waterman found that many of the organizational 
design solutions available to them and their clients only focused on structure and strategy 
when dealing with organizational issues. They found that this limited focus never 
allowed organizations to completely solve their problems or set them up entirely for 
success. 
The 7-S Model is “a conceptual framework useful in diagnosing the causes of 
organizational malaise and in formulating programs for improvement”[49], [50]. Peters 
and Waterman believed “that effective organizational change is really the relationship 
between structure, strategy, systems, style, skills, staff,” and superordinate goals [50]. 
These 7-Ss are what constitute their framework. The McKinsey 7-S Model is shown below 
in Figure 3.  

31 
 
 
 
 
Figure 3: McKinsey 7-S Model [51] 
Structure is an organization’s ability to focus on the elements of the organization’s 
design that are most important to the future growth of the organization [49].  
Strategy is any set of plans that guide how the organization should respond to (or 
anticipates) changes to its operating environment.   
Systems are the processes and procedures that organizations use to accomplish 
their work.  
Style is the “tangible evidence of what management considers important by the 
way it collectively spends time and attention and uses symbolic behavior. It is not what 
management says is important; it is the way management behaves”[51].  
Skills are an organization's capabilities, and these should not be confused with 
individual member skills and expertise.  
Staff are the members of the organization.  

32 
 
 
 
 
Shared Values are the “guiding concepts—a set of values and aspirations, often 
unwritten, that go beyond the conventional formal statement of corporate objectives. 
They are the broad notions of future direction the top management team wants to infuse 
throughout the organization”[50]. Another term Peters and Waterman use to explain 
shared values is superordinate goals. 
Three less apparent elements of their framework, which are only evident in the 
graphical depiction, are the seven elements together, the diagram itself, and the shape of 
the diagram. The seven elements together are intended to convey multiplicity and the 
notion that there are several “factors that influence an organization’s ability to change 
and its proper mode of change”[50]. They believed that the seven elements must be in 
unison with each other for the organization's design to succeed.  
In addition, the diagram symbolizes the interconnectedness of the elements and 
the idea that they must all be addressed in the organizational design process.  Another 
less obvious element is the shape of the diagram. This is significant because it highlights 
that there is no specific starting point and that all elements must be addressed together. 
2.2.3.2.1 McKinsey 7-S Model Theoretical Background 
 
Although this model was not produced within academia, Peters and Waterman 
were still influenced by several aspects of organizational theory when they developed 
their 7-S Model.  Peters and Waterman drew on the work of Chester Barnard. Barnard’s 
work focused on how management is a social skill and how it is the manager's 
responsibility to ensure that the workers are focused on the organization’s goals [35]. This 
aspect of organizational theory shows up in the 7-S Model through the style element, 
which is about how management influences the workforce, specifically through their 
behavior. 
 
Additionally, based on Peters and Waterman’s assertion, “organization 
effectiveness stems from the interaction of several factors—some not especially obvious 
and some under-analyzed”[50]. It is clear they were influenced by systems theory and 
the idea that the system is greater than the sum of its parts; in this case, the organization 
is the system, and its parts are the seven elements; only when those seven elements are 
aligned, will the organization function in an optimal way.  
 
2.2.3.2.2 McKinsey 7-S Model Application 
Peters and Waterman believed their model would help diagnose and solve 
organizational problems. It is also a framework that allows organizations to take a holistic 
approach to addressing organizational design issues, and it can be used when developing 
organizational designs.   

33 
 
 
 
 
 
Peters and Waterman acknowledge that organizations can take two primary 
approaches when applying their model. Organizations can take a systematic and 
thoughtful approach and use the model in great detail, or they can take a more high-level 
approach. They were so confident in their framework that they suggested a “checklist” 
approach to the model would have powerful effects for an organization and it would 
allow leaders “to understand how organizations really operate” and even allow them “to 
design a truly comprehensive change program” [51].   
2.2.3.2.3 McKinsey 7-S Model Strengths, Limitations and Critiques  
 
A strength of the McKinsey 7-S Model, and what sets it apart from Galbraith’s Star 
Model, is its recognition of culture. Waterman explains that “the 7-S Framework is saying 
that culture is at least a function of seven variables”[50]. Although it is not explicitly its 
own element, culture can be teased out from the “soft” elements: style, skills, staff, and 
shared values. Another strength of the model is its attempt to force the organization to 
look at itself through various elements. The seven aspects of the model allow leaders and 
managers to take a broader perspective of their organization.  
 
Although the McKinsey 7-S model strives to be comprehensive, there are 
limitations to its application and practicality.  The first limitation is that “there are no 
external factors” involved in the model; the emphasis is on internal elements only [52]. 
As noted previously, the environment plays a crucial role in an organization’s 
performance; a lack of a clear acknowledgment of it in the model is concerning. 
 
Despite the model's relatively simple visual, many parameters need to be 
considered, such as the seven factors, the interconnectedness, and the lack of a clear 
starting point. These elements can make using the model difficult and even overwhelm 
the user due to all the things they need to consider as they design or redesign their 
organization. 
 
Finally, the model does not provide guidance on routine or continuous adaptation. 
Perhaps this shortcoming further highlights the lack of consideration for the 
organization’s operating environment, but whether it is today or the late 1970s, the world 
is constantly changing, and operating environments are becoming less and less 
predictable. Not considering how to continually scan and adjust an organization based 
on external factors is another limitation of the model. 
2.2.3.3 Burke-Litwin Model 
 
In 1992, W. Warner Burke and George H. Litwin published their seminal work 
entitled A Causal Model of Organizational Performance and Change; in this paper, they put 
forth their model of organizational function and organizational change. The goal of their 
model was “to provide a causal framework that encompasses both the what and the how—

34 
 
 
 
 
what organizational dimensions are key to successful change and how these dimensions 
should be linked causally to achieve the change goals”[53]. The Burke-Litwin Model is 
shown below in Figure 4.  
Figure 4: Burke-Litwin Model [53] 
 
 
As evident in Figure 4, this model is complex. Burke and Litwin recognized this 
and claimed that although the model is “complex to depict and describe, it is still an 
oversimplification” [53]. Figure 4 shows the key factors that Burke and Litwin theorized 
to influence an organization’s behavior and how they interact with each other to drive 
change.  

35 
 
 
 
 
 
Before delving further into the model's details, it is important to highlight two 
primary concepts that shape it. The Burke-Litwin model shows “two distinct sets of 
organizational dynamics. One set is primarily associated with the transactional level of 
human behavior or the everyday interactions and exchanges that create the climate of the 
organization. The second set of dynamics is concerned with processes of human 
transformation, amounting to sudden ‘leaps’ in behavior” [53].  Burke and Litwin 
indicated that the transactional level of change is handled by management, and the 
transformational level is led by leadership [53]. It is important to note, that Burke and 
Litwin considered leadership to be the executive level positions of an organization who 
were responsible for overall direction of the organization and management to be the 
lower levels responsible for the day-to-day operations.  
  
The transactional factors are structure, management practices, systems (policies 
and procedures), work unit climate, task and individual skills, motivation, individual 
needs and values, and individual and organizational performance. 
• Structure is how the organization is organized.  
• Management practices are the reoccurring actions and decisions made to ensure 
the organization achieves its goals.  
• Systems are the policies and procedures that should be followed to support the 
organization in achieving its goals.   
• Climate is the mood and atmosphere of the organization and how it influences 
employee behavior and interactions.  
• Task requirements and individual skills/abilities are the skills, knowledge, and 
behavior needed to accomplish employees’ jobs.   
• Individual needs and values are the personal factors that influence an employee’s 
actions.   
• Motivation is the drive and willingness to contribute to the organization’s mission 
and goal accomplishment.  
• Individual and organizational performance results from how well an employee or 
the organization is doing.   
  
The transformational factors are the external environment, mission and strategy, 
leadership, and organizational culture.  
• The external environment is the outside factors that impact the performance of an 
organization.   
• Mission and strategy represent the purpose and plans to direct the organization.  
• Leadership are the top-level executives who provide direction to the organization.  

36 
 
 
 
 
• Culture is considered the organization's written and unwritten rules, values, and 
principles.  
 
 Another element that needs to be addressed is the use of arrows. These arrows 
highlight essential linkages between the elements and, more importantly, demonstrate 
the open system principle, which is the idea that the environment influences the 
organization and that a feedback loop exists between the two.  
  
Burke and Litwin believed that by displaying their model in this manner, they 
could make “a statement about organizational change. Organizational change, especially 
an overhaul of the company business strategy, stems more from the environmental 
impact than from any other factor” [53]. Additionally, they believed that the 
transformation factors had more impact than the transactional factors.  
2.2.3.3.1 Burke-Litwin Model Theoretical Background 
 
 The Burke-Litwin Model draws on two primary aspects of organizational theory: 
systems theory and contingency theory. The model takes a systems theory approach by 
recognizing the environment and how the organization responds to it or more simply put 
as feedback and control. The model emphasizes the twelve elements and their alignment 
to optimize organizational performance. This approach draws from contingency theory 
and the work of Lawrence and Lorsch, which is precisely the idea that the organization 
must match the conditions the environment creates. 
2.2.3.3.2 Burke-Litwin Model Application 
  
The Burke-Litwin model “is a best-known and most influential model for looking 
at the role of organizational climate in business performance” for an organization [54], 
[55]. The Burke-Litwin model can also be used to design or redesign an organization, 
guide change management, diagnose problems, and assess performance improvement 
opportunities.  
 
Burke and Litwin posit that their model could be used in parts: (a) if an 
organization wants to undergo a significant change, it should focus on “the top 
transformational boxes” and its associated elements for that change [53] and (b) if an 
organization wants to address internal processes and efficiencies, it should focus on the 
lower level of the model and use the transactional elements to guide the process. Finally, 
the model can be used as a whole to help leadership and management undergo a 
complete transformation of an organization.   

37 
 
 
 
 
2.2.3.3.3 Burke-Litwin Model Strengths, Limitations and Critiques  
 
The strengths of the Burke-Litwin Model are its comprehensiveness, flexibility to 
be used in parts or as a whole, and recognition of the causal relationships that occur 
during organizational design or redesign. Martins and Coetzee noted that two strengths 
of the model are the recognition of the relationship between the internal organization and 
its external environment and that it differentiates the role of transformational and 
transactional dynamics in the organization. Additionally, some have lauded the model 
for being “more than merely descriptive and congruent; it serves as a guide not only for 
organizational diagnosis but also for planned, managed organizational change[56]. 
 
A significant limitation and critique of the Burke-Litwin Model is its complexity 
and the amount of elements and considerations that must be made while using it [54]. 
The twelve elements and the arrows could overwhelm practitioners and even lead to a 
misapplication of the model. Despite recognizing the importance of the environment, 
some have taken issue with how the environment is shown in the model. Spangenberg 
and Theron stated, “this positioning may create the impression that the external 
environment controls organizational leaders”[57]. Finally, the model is static and does 
not provide any guidance on how organizations can use it if they exist in unstable 
environments. 
2.2.3.4 Organizational Models Comparison 
 
The Galbraith’s Star Model, the McKinsey 7-S Model, and the Burke-Litwin Model 
are commonly used models for designing or redesigning organizations.  While each 
model is distinct and has its unique approach, they all share common organizational 
design principles.  
The similarities between the three models are that they emphasize several 
elements at play when it comes to organizational design and redesign; they all recognize 
that these elements need to be aligned for organizational effectiveness. All three models 
are agnostic to the type of organization to which it can be applied and when it can be 
applied.  
Key differences amongst the models are the number of elements recognized in 
each model; Galbraith’s Star Model has five components, McKinsey 7-S Model has seven 
components, and Burke-Litwin has twelve components. Although they all can be used 
for organizational design and redesign, their focuses are nuanced. Galbraith’s Star Model 
is focused on aligning strategy with the other elements, McKinsey's 7-S Model is focused 
on internal alignment of the organization, and Burke-Litwin is focused on assessing and 
managing organizational change through transformational and transactional views.  

38 
 
 
 
 
While all these models help develop organizational design options, they are 
insufficient for our ever-changing and complex world. All three models draw on systems 
theory and thinking in their approach, yet a closer analysis reveals that they fall short of 
applying true systems theory principles. These three models primarily take a reductionist 
approach; through their elements, such as structure, strategy, and motivation, they break 
an organization down into low-level components without recognizing the complexity of 
these interdependencies at the organizational level. Their emphasis on elements results 
in an isolated focus instead of a holistic look at the organization, as systems theory 
requires, which leads to an incomplete understanding of the organization.  
Additionally, these models do not account for nonlinear interactions and emergent 
properties that occur in complex systems like organizations; these models are static and 
fail to truly capture the dynamic nature of organizations. Their application reflects a 
component-based view rather than an actual systems theory perspective.  
A more nuanced systems theoretic lens is needed to design and redesign 
organizations. The following section expands in much greater detail on Systems Theory 
and various systems-theoretic approaches for system analysis.  
2.3 Systems Theory  
 
Systems Theory has been developed in the last half-century to enable insight and 
analysis into increasingly complex systems. Specifically, it allows the understanding of 
systems that exhibit organized complexity, which is “too complex for complete analysis 
and too organized for statistics” [58], [59]. Complex systems can be natural, engineered, 
or social systems like an organization. Common examples include the following: the 
ecosystem of a river, the Lockheed Martin F-35 Lightning II Supersonic Stealth Strike 
Fighter, and the Federal Food and Drug Administration.  
 
According to Gerald Weinberg, author of the seminal book An Introduction into 
General Systems Thinking, systems that exhibit organized complexity demand more 
holistic analysis techniques [58]. This need for holistic analysis stems from the idea that 
some system properties, such as safety, effectiveness, and efficiency, can only be fully 
understood by considering all aspects of the system. These properties emerge from how 
the different parts of the system interact; therefore, systems that exhibit organized 
complexity should be viewed and analyzed as a whole and not decomposed into separate 
parts for analysis [59], [60]. Systems Theory provides a framework for understanding 
complex systems, specifically focusing on a holistic understanding of the dynamic 
relationships that drive system-level properties.  
  
The two main principles of Systems theory are as follows: 1) emergence and 
hierarchy and 2) communication and control [5]. Emergence and hierarchy as a principle 

39 
 
 
 
 
means that a system can be viewed in hierarchical levels, with each subsequent higher 
level exhibiting increasing complexity. The concept of emergence means that the 
behaviors and properties inherent to a single level of complexity within a system cannot 
be analyzed below that level of abstraction. Communication and control imply that any 
higher level within a system can apply controls to lower levels within the system. This 
concept of implementing control constraints on behavior at the lower level affects 
changes in that lower level’s emergent behavior. These two principles apply to any 
technical or even purely social system. In addition to these two principles, several 
foundational concepts within Systems Theory exist. These are summarized below in 
Table 3. 
Table 3: Systems Theory Concepts 
Systems Theory Concepts 
Concept 
Explanation 
System 
A set of components that act together as a whole to achieve some common goal, 
objective, or end [61].  
Hierarchical 
Levels 
These are the layers of organization within a system. The higher the level, the more 
complexity it exhibits.   
Component  
These are the elements that make up a system. In an engineered system, this could be 
the body of an aircraft, its electrical system, and its engine. In a social system like an 
organization, these could be an organization's individuals, groups, or departments.  
Boundary 
What separates a system from its environment [62]. A boundary can be physical, 
conceptual, or both.  
Environment 
Everything outside the system’s boundary.  
Open 
Systems  
These systems interact with the environment and adapt to external changes to 
maintain equilibrium.  
Inputs, 
Processes, 
Outputs 
The flow of resources and information into a system which is then processed through 
some action and produces output such as results or products.  
Feedback 
A circular process into which the output of a system is fed back into a system, which 
allows the systems to adapt and respond to changes as necessary.  
Holism  
The idea is that the system must be studied as a whole, not decomposed and analyzed 
as separate parts.  
Sources: [59], [62], [63]  

40 
 
 
 
 
  
Systems Theory provides guiding principles for understanding and analyzing 
complex systems. Systems Theory and its emphasis on focusing on the system as a whole 
is a significant paradigm shift from other theories. As a theory, it enables analysis and 
synthesis

title: Application of causal analysis based on systems theory (CAST) to regulatory decision-making: A case study of the Sikorsky S92A
abstract_summary: This study applies CAST (Causal Analysis based on Systems Theory) to examine how the Sikorsky S92A operates in offshore elevated helideck environments despite not being certified for such operations. The analysis reveals unsafe decisions by flight crews, operators, manufacturers, and regulators that create a gap between aircraft certification and actual operational use.
key_findings: 100% of surveyed S92A pilots in Brazil incorrectly believed their aircraft was certified for elevated helideck operations (54 out of 54 pilots)

The S92A operates primarily offshore (70% of deliveries) but is not certified for elevated helideck operations under 14 CFR Part 29, creating 9 seconds of exposure to catastrophic failure during takeoff/landing
Actual engine failure rates in some countries are over 2x higher than Sikorsky's published rate of 0.6 per 100,000 flight hours, invalidating safety assumptions used in regulatory exemptions

The FAA added explicit certification limitations to the S92A Type Certificate Data Sheet only 7 years after initial certification (2009), indicating widespread confusion about operational capabilities
methodology: CAST analysis applied to a hypothetical accident based on a real 2015 Service Difficulty Report involving S92A engine failure during hover. Five-step CAST process: (1) basic information assembly, (2) hierarchical control structure modeling, (3) individual controller contribution analysis, (4) systemic factor identification, (5) improvement recommendations.
limitations: Analysis based on hypothetical accident rather than actual investigation with full access to parties and records
Analysis scope limited to regulatory/certification issues, excluding technical engine failure causes
CAST analysis terminated at national regulatory level for conciseness, may have missed higher-level systemic factors

Prior research by Veras Neto and De Andrade (2022) identifying regulatory gaps in Transport Category rotorcraft certification vs. operation
notable_quotes: ICAO defines safety as 'the state in which risks associated with aviation activities, related to, or in direct support of the operation of aircraft, are reduced and controlled to an acceptable level'
The FAA recognizes that there may be instances in which a safe forced landing may not be possible due to environmental or other factors
Every second of delay in the pilot's reaction to an OEI condition at the TDP may cause a reduction of 15 ft of helideck edge clearance distance

software_dev_relevance.summary: This research directly informs how software systems handle certification vs. operational reality gaps. The core insight is that when certified capabilities don't match actual usage patterns, distributed teams develop conflicting mental models that lead to systematic safety violations - highly applicable to API versioning, security compliance frameworks, and production deployment practices.
specific_applications: API deprecation and breaking change management - teams may continue using deprecated APIs believing they're still supported, similar to pilots believing uncertified procedures are certified
Security compliance frameworks where development teams assume certain security controls are in place when they're actually exempted or incomplete
Production deployment pipelines where staging environment limitations don't match production requirements, leading to runtime failures
anti_patterns: Publishing uncertified documentation (like API examples or configuration templates) alongside certified documentation without clear distinction - creates false confidence in operational teams
Granting security or operational exemptions without establishing corresponding training, monitoring, or validation requirements

Application of causal analysis based on systems theory (CAST) to regulatory 
decision-making: A case study of the Sikorsky S92A
Clementino R. Veras Neto a, Rodrigo L. Rose b,*, John Thomas b

Keywords:
Rotorcraft certification
Rotorcraft operations
Performance classes
Aviation safety
Offshore operations
A B S T R A C T
Ensuring aviation safety requires maintaining the integrity of product design and operations. The Federal 
Aviation Administration (FAA) regulates Transport Category rotorcraft design through 14 CFR Part 29, estab­
lishing Categories A and B of certification for multiengine rotorcraft, and requires aircraft to be operated ac­
cording to the certified procedures in flight manuals. This paper presents a case study of the Sikorsky S92A, a 
Transport Category rotorcraft that is not certified for elevated helideck operations according to Part 29, but 
operates primarily in the offshore market through FAA-authorized exemptions from applicable regulation. To 
understand how this discrepancy between the aircraft’s certification and operation came to be, a relatively new 
accident analysis methodology called Casual Analysis based on Systems Theory (CAST) is applied to a hypo­
thetical accident involving an S92A, strongly based on a real incident described in a service difficulty report. The 
CAST results identify unsafe decisions on the part of flight crews, air operators, the aircraft manufacturer, and the 
FAA that contribute to the accident. We explain these contributions by identifying several systemic factors 
generalizable to the entire offshore rotorcraft industry that underlie unsafe decisions, and we propose a set of 
recommendations to address them.
1. Introduction
The main goal of any national Civil Aviation Authority is ensuring 
aviation safety. In line with this, the Federal Aviation Administration’s 
(FAA) mission includes “the issuance and enforcement of regulations and 
standards related to the manufacture, operation, certification and mainte­
nance of aircraft.” [1].
From a regulatory perspective, in order to achieve aviation safety 
two pillars are essential: product integrity and operational integrity. 
Product integrity involves design, certification, production, and quality 
assurance, among other factors, while integrity of operations involves 
but is not restricted to flight operations, crew training, minimum 
equipment lists, standard operating procedures, and ensuring continued 
airworthiness. There is an intrinsic relationship between product 
integrity and operational integrity that must be maintained in order to 
achieve continuous operational safety and, thereby, aviation safety as a 
whole [2] (Fig. 1).
The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) publishes 
Standards and Recommended Practices (SARPs) for different subject 
areas within aviation. SARPs are published by ICAO through 19 Annexes 
and are subject to regular amendments. In Annex 19, ICAO defines 
safety as “the state in which risks associated with aviation activities, related 
to, or in direct support of the operation of aircraft, are reduced and controlled 
to an acceptable level” [4].
Some regulations regarding rotorcraft certification and operation are 
applied before leaving the Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) 
gate (i.e., factory gate in), while other regulations are applied after the 
rotorcraft leaves the OEM’s gate (i.e., factory gate out). Some additional 
regulations are applied on both sides of the OEM’s gate. The relationship 
between ICAO Annexes and FAA regulations on both sides of the OEM’s

Helicopters are essential for supporting offshore oil and gas activities 
worldwide [5]. According to the International Association of Oil & Gas 
Producers (IOGP) [6], about 300,000 rotorcraft flight hours were 
registered across IOGP’s members in 2022. This is a downgrade from the 
over 400,000 flight hours in 2019, mainly as a result of the COVID-19 
pandemic, but this still accounts for the transportation of over 3.4 
million passengers annually.
Since a 2016 accident involving an Airbus H225/EC225 helicopter in 
the North Sea, the 19-passenger Sikorsky S92A [7] has dominated 
offshore air operations in the western hemisphere. In January 2016 
there were seventeen Airbus H225/EC225 and fifteen Sikorsky S92A in 
Brazilian offshore operations, while by February 2023 there was only 
one Airbus H225/EC225 and thirty-three Sikorsky S92A [8]. As seen in 
Fig. 3, in 2018 the S92 had the highest number of reported flight hours in 
offshore operation, as collected and reported by HeliOffshore [9].
Typically, an offshore flight consists of one takeoff or landing on land 
and one or more takeoffs or landings on oil rigs. This means that at least 
50% of all offshore takeoff and landing operations occur on elevated 
helidecks. Most offshore helicopter operations involve the trans­
portation of workers, so disruptions can lead to discontinuities in pro­
duction flows that can have severe social, economic and political 
impacts [5]. Though offshore helicopter operations generally pose 
higher risks than ground-based operations, statistical analyses regarding 
the safety of the offshore helicopter industry have shown lower accident 
rates in offshore operations, as a result of stricter regulation and tighter 
control both on the design and operational sides [10]. However, the 
offshore industry is not immune to safety concerns, and to ensure both 
product and operational integrity in the industry, it is essential that the 
environment in which these helicopters operate match the basis on 
which they were certified.
This study demonstrates an application of an accident analysis 
methodology called Causal Analysis based on Systems Theory (CAST) to 
a near miss involving the S92A, to model and understand a gap between 
the certification and operation of that helicopter in the offshore market. 
CAST is used to examine how interactions between flight crews, air 
operators, OEMs, and regulatory authorities allow the S92A to occa­
sionally operate in environments in which it is exposed to a higher 
likelihood of a catastrophic loss than is widely known and disseminated. 
The CAST findings are then used to propose recommendations for 
improving regulatory decision-making and offshore helicopter opera­
tions as a whole.
The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Section 2 out­
lines a literature review of the fundamentals of certification and oper­
ational regulation of transport category rotorcraft, Section 3 presents a 
brief description of CAST; Section 4 presents a summary of the results of 
a CAST applied to a near miss involving the S92A; Section 5 analyses the 
gaps uncovered in the CAST more deeply and provides recommenda­
tions for improving the safety of offshore operations; and Section 6
concludes the paper.
2. Background and literature review
2.1. Fundamentals of airworthiness and operations regulation
2.1.1. Airworthiness certification regulation for transport category 
rotorcraft
ICAO defines an aircraft as airworthy “when it conforms to its approved 
design and is in a condition for safe operation”, establishing the airwor­
thiness basis in Annex 8 – Airworthiness of Aircraft [11, p. 8].
In the USA, Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) 
establishes all rules prescribed by the FAA to control aviation activities. 
The certification requirements regarding the design of Transport Cate­
gory rotorcraft are set in 14 CFR Part 29 (Airworthiness Standards: 
Transport Category Rotorcraft) and are divided into Category A and 
Category B for multiengine rotorcraft. The requirements for Category A 
certification are more stringent than Category B [12].
According to the original version of 14 CFR Part 29, rotorcraft with a 
maximum takeoff weight (MTOW) greater than 20,000 lb had to be 
certified as Category A, while rotorcraft with a MTOW of 20,000 lb or 
less could be certified as Category B, as shown in Fig. 4(a).
Each certification category also possesses different operating limi­
tations [12]. For example, to be certified as Category A, a rotorcraft must 
prove it is capable of continued safe flight with critical engine failure at 
any point during the flight path. Category B certification does not 
require the rotorcraft to be capable of taking off, continuing flight, or 
landing at the intended destination in the event of an engine failure. A 
rotorcraft certified to Category B is therefore assumed to perform an

In 1983, the FAA published Amendment 29–21 to Part 29 [13]. This 
amendment removed the 20,000 lb weight limit for Category B and 
removed the HV envelope as an operating limitation for rotorcraft car­
rying up to 9 passengers. This change created, in practice, three certifi­
cation categories for transport category rotorcraft with MTOW over 6, 
000 lb (revised to 7,000 lb in 1999): one pure Category A, one pure 
Category B, and one ‘hybrid’ Category [2], as can be seen in Fig. 4(b).
In the ‘hybrid’ category [2], rotorcraft capable of carrying 10 or more 
passengers and with a MTOW up to 20,000 lb must comply with all 
requirements of Category B certification and, additionally, the following 
two performance requirements of Category A certification: 
• Part 29, §29.67(a)(2) – 2nd segment of Category A takeoff OEI, from 
200 to 1000 ft above the surface, with rate of climb of 150ft/min at 
Vy; and
• Part 29, §§29.87 and 29.1517 – forbidden HV envelope, where any 
combination of height and forward velocity, including hover, within 
which it is not possible to make a safe landing following power 
failure of the critical engine.
Within Category A certification, there are also three different profiles 
for which a helicopter can be certified: clear area, ground heliport and 
elevated heliport. In the clear area profile, shown in Fig. 5, takeoff is 
typically horizontal. The takeoff decision point (TDP), that is, the point 
at which the takeoff can no longer be aborted, is usually defined in terms 
of indicated airspeed, as is typical for fixed-wing aircraft. In ground and 
elevated heliports, shown in Figs. 6 and 7 respectively, takeoff is typi­
cally vertical and the TDP is usually defined in terms of height over the 
takeoff surface. The main difference between ground and elevated he­
liports is that, in elevated heliports, the rotorcraft may descend below 
the level of the takeoff surface while attaining the takeoff safety speed 
(VTOSS) [12].
The reasons why operations over elevated helipads/helidecks are 
intrinsically more risky than over clear areas or ground helipads is due to 
the expected existence of obstacles in the vicinity and crosswind during 
takeoff/landings, particularly in offshore operations. Additionally, the 
helipad dimensions may be reduced down to the helicopter’s d-value 
(maximum helicopter dimension). The TDP height may also be reduced 
to just 30 ft above the helideck surface, due to the risk of the pilot losing 
sight of the helideck and being unable to reject the takeoff in the event of 
one engine becoming inoperative. Every second of delay in the pilot’s 
reaction to an OEI condition at the TDP may cause a reduction of 15 ft of 
helideck edge clearance distance [14]. The HeliOffshore report refer­
enced earlier [9] also provides statistics around helicopter safety in 
offshore operations and a summary of documented accidents.
The FAA does not require specific practices to demonstrate that a 
helicopter complies with 14 CFR Part 29. However, as guidance for 
OEMs, the FAA does provide advisory circulars (ACs) that outline

2.1.2. Operational regulation for transport category rotorcraft
In 1986, ICAO published Annex 6 Part III, titled Operation of Aircraft 
– International Commercial Air Transport — Helicopters [18, p. 6]. That 
Annex states that every helicopter “shall be operated in accordance with a 
code of performance established by the State of the Operator, in compliance 
with the applicable Standards of this chapter” [19, p. 6]. This means that 
each individual country’s civil aviation authority (CAA) is responsible 
for ensuring that rotorcraft in that country operate in accordance with a 
‘Code of Performance’ established by the CAA.
To serve as a basis for the code of performance, Annex 6 Part III 
defines three ‘Performance Classes’, which are sets of rules that pre­
scribe helicopter operational performance requirements when operating 
in each class. With one engine inoperative (OEI), the requirements for 
operating in Performance Class 1 (PC1) are equivalent to the certifica­
tion requirements for Category A. The requirements for operating in 
Performance Class 2 (PC2) are equivalent to the certification re­
quirements of the ‘hybrid’ Category certification, (i.e., Category B dur­
ing takeoff/landings and Category A enroute and in the 2nd segment 
takeoff OEI). The requirements for operating in Performance Class 3

2.2. The Gap between offshore helicopter certification and operations
Previous research on offshore helicopter operations in the oil and gas 
industry were mostly focused on operational safety [5,22], logistical 
improvements in transportation [23,24], and statistical analysis of ac­
cident data [25,26,27,28].
In a 2022 paper, Veras Neto and De Andrade [2] compared the 
certification and operation of Transport Category rotorcraft, first iden­
tifying a regulatory gap that exists for some helicopters primarily used in 
the oil and gas industry. That study found that a number of Transport 
Category rotorcraft operating in the offshore market, including the 
Sikorsky S92A and Airbus H225/EC225, are not certified to operate 
from elevated helidecks. The procedures for elevated helideck vertical 
take-off and landing presented in these helicopters’ rotorcraft flight 
manual (RFM) are not certified or approved by the FAA [12] or EASA 
[29] under their relevant certification regulations. To allow the heli­
copters to operate in this regime, the FAA grants operators exemptions, 
as described in Section 2.1.2.
As a result, a helicopter operating from an elevated helideck at a 
takeoff or landing weight consistent with the MTOW for Performance 
Class 2 (PC2) would not actually be covered by the safety assurances 
provided by Category A certification. In reality, during each takeoff and 
landing from an elevated helideck in the event of the critical engine fails, 
for a period of up to 9 s after the TDP, the helicopter would be exposed to 
the possibility of a deck-edge strike, or an emergency forced landing 
with obstacles on the surface, rather than a safe flyaway as required by 
Category A or a safe forced landing (SFL) as required by Category B.
The CAST results presented in Section 4 of this article attempt to 
understand how this gap formed by examining one instance of a critical 
engine failure at takeoff involving a Sikorsky S92A.
3. Method
3.1. The stamp framework
The System Theoretic Accident Model and Processes (STAMP) is a 
framework for understanding accident causality that is underpinned by 
systems theory [30]. In STAMP, safety is viewed as an emergent prop­
erty of complex systems, and the only way to prevent accidents is to 
enforce the appropriate controls on a system’s behavior. These controls, 
typically termed safety constraints, can include physical controls like 
closing a valve, but they can also include organizational constraints like 
procedures and training. Knowing when and how to enforce these 
constraints requires appropriate information, termed feedback. The 
feedback-control loop is the basic unit of a system model in STAMP. Also, 
in STAMP, a system does not simply refer to a physical system like a 
landing gear or even a whole aircraft. In STAMP, a system includes 
operators, management, and even regulatory authorities that all have 
control over the behavior of the physical components.
3.2. Causal analysis based on systems theory (CAST)
Causal Analysis based on Systems Theory (CAST) [31] is an accident 
analysis technique based on the STAMP framework. A detailed overview 
of CAST is found in the CAST Handbook [31]. The goal of CAST is to 
provide a structured approach that guides experts to think in more depth 
about the causes of an accident and generate better recommendations to 
prevent similar accidents in the future. CAST can also be applied to near 
misses, or any undesired situation, even if no loss was actually incurred.
CAST differs from traditional accident analysis techniques as it does 
not seek to identify a single “root cause” for the accident. Instead, CAST 
models the system involved in the accident as a collection of feedback 
control loops (termed a control structure) and examines each individual 
controller to understand their contributions to the accident. Rather than 
stop at each contribution, though, CAST goes on to identify why it 
appeared reasonable for each controller to make the decisions they 
made, even if those decisions were unsafe in hindsight. CAST also does 
not assign blame for an accident to any component, individual, or or­
ganization within the system. Instead, it focuses on understanding why 
the safety constraints were not enforced appropriately and generating 
recommendations to ensure they are enforced in the future.
The five steps of CAST involve: (1) assembling the basic information 
about the accident; (2) modeling the system involved as a hierarchical 
control structure; (3) analyzing each controller for their contributions to 
the accident; (4) analyzing the control structure as a whole to identify 
systemic factors affecting the behavior of all controllers; and (5) creating 
an improvement plan to prevent future accidents. For brevity, the CAST 
example in this study will only summarize the results from steps 1, 2, 3 
and 5.
4. Results
4.1. Summary of the case
The incident being examined using CAST in this study is based on a 
real incident that occurred on May 4th, 2015 and was documented in a 
Service Difficulty Report submitted to the FAA. The text of the report 
reads: 
“(CAN) NR 2 ENGINE FAILED WHILE IN THE HOVER, OVER THE 
RUNWAY, JUST PRIOR TO ROTATING FOR THE TAKEOFF. THE 
ACFT WAS LANDED. THE RT SEAT PILOT HEARD 2 QUICK POPS 
AND NOTICED THE TGT ON NR 2 RISE JUST PRIOR TO ENGINE 
FAILURE. THE WEATHER WAS SKY CLEAR WITH WINDS 
APPROXIMATELY 300 AT 10 KNOTS AND TEMPERATURE 13. THE 
ACFT WAS TAXIED BACK TO THE RAMP WITHOUT FURTHER 
INCIDENT.”
The SDR indicates that this incident occurred in the FAA’s southwest 
region (encompassing the states of Arkansas, Louisiana, Texas, Okla­
homa, and New Mexico). The mention of a “ramp” in the narrative 
implies the incident did not occur in an elevated helideck environment, 
although it could have occurred in the 9 second window mentioned 
earlier, as it occurred during the hover checks that precede rotation for 
takeoff from clear areas. Additionally, there is little information on the 
number of passengers in the aircraft at the time of the incident, or its 
takeoff weight.
Fortunately, no catastrophic accident resulted from this sudden en­
gine shutdown. However, in a scenario in which that same shutdown 
occurred up to 9 s after the TDP during a takeoff from an elevated hel­
ideck, in an aircraft at its full capacity of 21 occupants, the rapid loss of 
helideck edge clearance discussed earlier combined with crosswind and 
potential obstacles could lead to a higher reduction in safety margins. 
Based on the gap uncovered by Veras Neto and De Andrade as described 
in Section 2.2, that same shutdown in those conditions would result in a 
crash over the helideck, a crash over the sea following a tail strike on the 
helideck-edge, or a forced landing with low chances of survivability, if 
operating over hostile water conditions. Therefore, the CAST results 
presented in the next subsection will examine a hypothetical accident 
similar to the incident described in the SDR. In the hypothetical accident 
analyzed, the engine loss occurs up to 9 s after the TDP during a takeoff 
from an elevated helideck, leading to the catastrophic consequences 
described above.
It is important to note that, because the focus of this paper is on the 
regulatory gap, the focus will be on the decision-making at the operator, 
OEM, and regulator levels, rather than on the technical causes of the 
engine shutdown. Those technical causes are outside the scope of this
